rationale:
Split into two independent children (no sibling dependencies). Each matches a block of the supplied proof.

(1) density_representation covers supplied steps 3, 5, 6 and 7.
- It is a genuinely reusable lemma: the supplied proof already phrases these steps for a generic ξ ∈ {aᵢ, bᵢ} with ξ ≪ μ₀, and uses them 2m times (ξ = aᵢ and ξ = bᵢ for every i).
- It is the Lebesgue–Radon–Nikodym theorem in integral form for compact-finite measures on a σ-compact space (cf. Rudin, Real and Complex Analysis, Thm 6.10; Folland, Real Analysis, Thm 3.8).

(2) dominating_measure covers supplied steps 2 and 4.
- It is an independent standard fact: a finite family of compact-finite measures is dominated by its sum, and the sum is compact-finite.

How the children imply the selected statement (supplied steps 1, 8, 9, 10):
- Put bᵢ := RealRMK.rieszMeasure Λ₁ᵢ and aᵢ := RealRMK.rieszMeasure Λ₂ᵢ. They are regular, hence IsFiniteMeasureOnCompacts. integral_rieszMeasure gives ∫ f dbᵢ = Λ₁ᵢ f and ∫ f daᵢ = Λ₂ᵢ f (Riesz–Markov–Kakutani; Rudin Thm 2.14, Folland Thm 7.2).
- Apply dominating_measure to the families (a, b) to obtain μ₀, compact-finite, with aᵢ ≪ μ₀ and bᵢ ≪ μ₀.
- Apply density_representation to (μ₀, aᵢ) and to (μ₀, bᵢ), choosing densities gaᵢ and gbᵢ for each i.
- Set ρᵢ := gbᵢ − gaᵢ. It is measurable (Measurable.sub) and integrable on every compact set (IntegrableOn.sub).
- For f ∈ C_c: Λ₁ᵢ f − Λ₂ᵢ f = ∫ f dbᵢ − ∫ f daᵢ = ∫ f·gbᵢ dμ₀ − ∫ f·gaᵢ dμ₀ = ∫ (f·gbᵢ − f·gaᵢ) dμ₀ = ∫ f·ρᵢ dμ₀. The third equality is integral_sub, using the integrability that density_representation supplies; the last is ring.

subproblems.title: Common dominating compact-finite measure for two finite families of compact-finite measures
subproblems.statement: Let X be a topological space equipped with a σ-algebra; no compatibility between the two is assumed. Let m ∈ ℕ and let a, b : Fin m → Measure X be two families of measures on X, each of which is finite on compact sets. Then there is a measure μ₀ on X that is finite on compact sets and satisfies aᵢ ≪ μ₀ and bᵢ ≪ μ₀ for every i ∈ Fin m.
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (X : Type) [TopologicalSpace X] [MeasurableSpace X] (m : ℕ) (a b : Fin m → Measure X), (∀ i, IsFiniteMeasureOnCompacts (a i)) → (∀ i, IsFiniteMeasureOnCompacts (b i)) → ∃ μ₀ : Measure X, IsFiniteMeasureOnCompacts μ₀ ∧ (∀ i, a i ≪ μ₀) ∧ ∀ i, b i ≪ μ₀
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source: steps 2 and 4 of the parent's supplied proof (the dominating measure μ₀ := Σᵢ (aᵢ + bᵢ) and absolute continuity), stated for arbitrary families of compact-finite measures. The parent applies it with aᵢ := RealRMK.rieszMeasure Λ₂ᵢ and bᵢ := RealRMK.rieszMeasure Λ₁ᵢ.
Hypotheses:
- X is a topological space with a σ-algebra; no compatibility is assumed or needed.
- m ∈ ℕ.
- a, b : Fin m → Measure X, with every aᵢ and every bᵢ finite on compact sets.

1. (Definition of μ₀.) Let μ₀ := Σ_{i ∈ Fin m} (aᵢ + bᵢ), the finite sum over Finset.univ of the measures aᵢ + bᵢ in the additive commutative monoid of measures on X. For m = 0 it is the zero measure. Evaluating a measure at a set commutes with sums of two measures (Measure.add_apply) and with finite sums of measures (Measure.finsetSum_apply). Both identities hold for every set s ⊆ X, measurable or not. Hence for every s ⊆ X:
 μ₀(s) = Σ_{i ∈ Fin m} (aᵢ(s) + bᵢ(s)) in [0, ∞]. (★)
2. (μ₀ is finite on compact sets.) Let K ⊆ X be compact and i ∈ Fin m.
 - aᵢ(K) < ∞ and bᵢ(K) < ∞, because aᵢ and bᵢ are finite on compact sets (IsFiniteMeasureOnCompacts.lt_top_of_isCompact).
 - Hence aᵢ(K) + bᵢ(K) < ∞ (ENNReal.add_lt_top).
 - A finite sum in [0, ∞] whose terms are all < ∞ is itself < ∞ (ENNReal.sum_lt_top). By (★), μ₀(K) < ∞.
 Since K was arbitrary, μ₀ is finite on compact sets.
3. (aᵢ ≪ μ₀ and bᵢ ≪ μ₀.) Fix i ∈ Fin m and a set s ⊆ X with μ₀(s) = 0.
 - By (★), Σ_{j ∈ Fin m} (aⱼ(s) + bⱼ(s)) = 0.
 - [0, ∞] is a canonically ordered additive monoid, so a finite sum is 0 iff each term is 0 (Finset.sum_eq_zero_iff). Taking j = i ∈ Finset.univ gives aᵢ(s) + bᵢ(s) = 0.
 - By the same principle for two summands (add_eq_zero), aᵢ(s) = 0 and bᵢ(s) = 0.
 In Mathlib, aᵢ ≪ μ₀ means every set of μ₀-measure 0 has aᵢ-measure 0. Since s was an arbitrary μ₀-null set, aᵢ ≪ μ₀ and bᵢ ≪ μ₀.
4. By steps 2 and 3, μ₀ is finite on compact sets and aᵢ ≪ μ₀, bᵢ ≪ μ₀ for every i ∈ Fin m. This proves the claim.
proof_key_steps: Define μ₀ := Σ_{i ∈ Fin m} (aᵢ + bᵢ). By Measure.finsetSum_apply and Measure.add_apply, μ₀(s) = Σᵢ (aᵢ(s) + bᵢ(s)) for every set s.
For compact K each aᵢ(K) and bᵢ(K) is finite, so μ₀(K) is a finite sum of finite terms and is finite (ENNReal.add_lt_top, ENNReal.sum_lt_top).
If μ₀(s) = 0, every summand vanishes (Finset.sum_eq_zero_iff, add_eq_zero), so aᵢ(s) = bᵢ(s) = 0. Hence aᵢ ≪ μ₀ and bᵢ ≪ μ₀.

subproblems.title: Locally integrable Radon–Nikodym density representing an absolutely continuous compact-finite measure on C_c
subproblems.statement: Let X be a locally compact Hausdorff space with a countable basis, equipped with its Borel σ-algebra. Let μ₀ and ξ be measures on X, both finite on compact sets, with ξ ≪ μ₀. Then there is a measurable function g : X → ℝ, μ₀-integrable on every compact subset of X, such that for every f ∈ C_c(X, ℝ) the function x ↦ f(x)·g(x) is μ₀-integrable and ∫ f dξ = ∫ f(x)·g(x) dμ₀(x).
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (X : Type) [TopologicalSpace X] [T2Space X] [LocallyCompactSpace X] [SecondCountableTopology X] [MeasurableSpace X] [BorelSpace X] (μ₀ ξ : Measure X), IsFiniteMeasureOnCompacts μ₀ → IsFiniteMeasureOnCompacts ξ → ξ ≪ μ₀ → ∃ g : X → ℝ, Measurable g ∧ (∀ K : Set X, IsCompact K → IntegrableOn g K μ₀) ∧ ∀ f : CompactlySupportedContinuousMap X ℝ, Integrable (fun x => f x * g x) μ₀ ∧ ∫ x, f x ∂ξ = ∫ x, f x * g x ∂μ₀
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source: steps 3, 5, 6 and 7 of the parent's supplied proof. They are already written for a single measure ξ ∈ {aᵢ, bᵢ} with ξ ≪ μ₀. Here μ₀ and ξ are arbitrary compact-finite measures with ξ ≪ μ₀. The parent applies the lemma 2m times, with ξ = aᵢ and ξ = bᵢ for each i ∈ Fin m.
Hypotheses:
- X is a locally compact Hausdorff space with a countable basis and its Borel σ-algebra. The Hausdorff hypothesis is not used below.
- μ₀ and ξ are measures on X, both finite on compact sets, with ξ ≪ μ₀.

1. (σ-finiteness and Lebesgue decomposition.)
 - X is locally compact with a countable basis, so it is σ-compact (sigmaCompactSpace_of_locallyCompact_secondCountable).
 - On a σ-compact space every measure that is finite on compact sets is σ-finite (SigmaFinite.of_isFiniteMeasureOnCompacts): X is the union of the countably many compact sets compactCovering X n, each of finite measure. So μ₀ and ξ are σ-finite.
 - In particular ξ is s-finite and μ₀ is σ-finite, so the pair (ξ, μ₀) has a Lebesgue decomposition (instance Measure.haveLebesgueDecomposition_of_sigmaFinite).
2. (The density δ.) Let δ := ξ.rnDeriv μ₀ : X → [0, ∞].
 - δ is measurable (Measure.measurable_rnDeriv).
 - The Lebesgue decomposition from step 1 gives ξ = ξ.singularPart μ₀ + μ₀.withDensity δ (Measure.haveLebesgueDecomposition_add).
 - Since ξ ≪ μ₀, the singular part vanishes: ξ.singularPart μ₀ = 0 (Measure.singularPart_eq_zero_of_ac). Hence ξ = μ₀.withDensity δ.
 - Since ξ is σ-finite, δ(x) < ∞ for μ₀-almost every x (Measure.rnDeriv_lt_top).
3. (Definition and measurability of g.) Define g : X → ℝ by g(x) := (δ x).toReal. g is measurable, as the composition of the measurable δ with the measurable map ENNReal.toReal (Measurable.ennreal_toReal).
4. (g is μ₀-integrable on every compact set.) Let K ⊆ X be compact.
 - ξ(K) < ∞, since ξ is finite on compact sets.
 - Measure.lintegral_rnDeriv_lt_top_of_measure_ne_top, applied with s = K (no measurability of K is required), gives ∫⁻_{x ∈ K} δ(x) dμ₀(x) < ∞.
 - δ is measurable, hence a.e.-measurable for μ₀ restricted to K.
 - integrable_toReal_of_lintegral_ne_top then shows that x ↦ (δ x).toReal = g(x) is integrable for μ₀ restricted to K, i.e. IntegrableOn g K μ₀.
5. (f·g is μ₀-integrable for f ∈ C_c(X, ℝ).) Let f ∈ C_c(X, ℝ).
 (i) f is continuous and X carries its Borel σ-algebra, so f is measurable (Continuous.measurable). In particular f is a.e.-strongly measurable for every measure.
 (ii) f has compact support, so K_f := tsupport f is compact. A continuous function with compact support is bounded: there is C ∈ ℝ with ‖f(x)‖ = |f(x)| ≤ C for all x ∈ X (Continuous.bounded_above_of_compact_support).
 (iii) By step 4, g is integrable for μ₀ restricted to K_f. Integrable.bdd_mul says that multiplying an integrable function by a bounded, a.e.-strongly measurable factor keeps it integrable. Apply it with factor f and the bound C, which holds everywhere and hence a.e. So x ↦ f(x)·g(x) is μ₀-integrable on K_f.
 (iv) For x ∉ K_f, f(x) = 0 (image_eq_zero_of_notMem_tsupport), hence f(x)·g(x) = 0. A function that is integrable on a set and vanishes at every point outside it is integrable (IntegrableOn.integrable_of_forall_notMem_eq_zero). So x ↦ f(x)·g(x) is μ₀-integrable.
6. (The integral identity.) Let f ∈ C_c(X, ℝ).
 - By step 2, ∫ f dξ = ∫ f d(μ₀.withDensity δ).
 - δ is measurable and δ < ∞ μ₀-a.e. (step 2), so integral_withDensity_eq_integral_toReal_smul gives ∫ f d(μ₀.withDensity δ) = ∫ (δ x).toReal • f(x) dμ₀(x) = ∫ g(x)·f(x) dμ₀(x).
 - Real multiplication is commutative, so g(x)·f(x) = f(x)·g(x) pointwise. Hence ∫ f dξ = ∫ f(x)·g(x) dμ₀(x).
7. By steps 3–6:
 - g is measurable and μ₀-integrable on every compact subset of X;
 - for every f ∈ C_c(X, ℝ), x ↦ f(x)·g(x) is μ₀-integrable and ∫ f dξ = ∫ f(x)·g(x) dμ₀(x).
 This proves the claim.
proof_key_steps: X is σ-compact, so the compact-finite measures μ₀ and ξ are σ-finite and (ξ, μ₀) has a Lebesgue decomposition.
δ := ξ.rnDeriv μ₀ is measurable. Since ξ ≪ μ₀, the singular part vanishes (singularPart_eq_zero_of_ac), so ξ = μ₀.withDensity δ; also δ < ∞ μ₀-a.e. (rnDeriv_lt_top).
g := (δ ·).toReal is measurable. For compact K, ξ(K) < ∞ gives ∫⁻_K δ dμ₀ < ∞, so g is integrable on K (integrable_toReal_of_lintegral_ne_top).
For f ∈ C_c(X, ℝ): f is measurable and bounded with compact tsupport, so f·g is integrable on tsupport f (Integrable.bdd_mul) and vanishes outside it, hence is μ₀-integrable.
integral_withDensity_eq_integral_toReal_smul gives ∫ f dξ = ∫ (δ x).toReal • f x dμ₀ = ∫ f x · g x dμ₀.
